Signal Discrimination Model (SDM)

Source: R/model_sdm.R
sdm.Rd

Signal Discrimination Model (SDM)

Usage

sdm(
  resp_error,
  version = "simple",
  activation = c("vonmises", "laplace"),
  scaling = NULL,
  ...
)

sdmSimple(resp_error, version = "simple", ...)

Arguments

resp_error

The name of the variable in the dataset containing the response error. The response error should code the response relative to the to-be-recalled target in radians. You can transform the response error in degrees to radians using the deg2rad function.

version

Character. The version of the model to use. Currently only "simple" is supported.

activation

Character. The activation kernel of the SDM, "vonmises" (the default, as in Oberauer, 2023) or "laplace". See the section "Activation functions".

scaling

Character. What the memory strength c measures: "density", "peak" or "range". NULL (the default) means "density" for the von Mises and "peak" for the Laplace activation. See the sections "Scaling of the activation" and "What c means".

...

used internally for testing, ignore it

Value

An object of class bmmodel

Details

see the online article for a detailed description of the model and how to use it. * Domain: Working memory

  • Task: Continuous reproduction

  • Name: Signal Discrimination Model (SDM)

  • Citation:

    • Oberauer, K. (2023). Measurement models for visual working memory—A factorial model comparison. Psychological Review, 130(3), 841-852. https://doi.org/10.1037/rev0000328

  • Version: simple

  • Requirements:

    • The response variable should be in radians and represent the angular error relative to the target

  • Parameters:

    • mu: Location parameter of the SDM distribution (in radians; by default fixed internally to 0)

    • c: Memory strength parameter of the SDM distribution

    • kappa: Precision parameter of the SDM distribution

  • Fixed parameters:

    • mu = 0

  • Default parameter links:

    • mu = tan_half; c = log; kappa = log

  • Default priors:

    • mu:

      • main: normal(0, 0.5)

      • effects: normal(0, 0.25)

      • sd: exponential(4)

    • kappa:

      • main: student_t(5, 1.75, 0.75)

      • effects: normal(0, 1)

      • sd: exponential(1)

    • c:

      • main: student_t(5, 2, 0.75)

      • effects: normal(0, 1)

      • sd: exponential(1)

Activation functions

Each response \(x\) is activated by \(c^* s(x - \mu)\), where the activation function \(s\) is 1 at the target and \(c^*\) is the activation of the target; the response density is \(\exp(c^* s(x - \mu)) / Z\), with \(Z\) its integral over the circle.

  • activation = "vonmises": \(s(x) = \exp(\kappa (\cos x - 1))\), the von Mises activation kernel of the signal discrimination model of Oberauer (2023).

  • activation = "laplace": \(s(x) = \exp(-\kappa |x|)\), with \(|x|\) the angular distance and \(\kappa\) the rate of the Laplace activation in Oberauer (2023, eq. 2). This is the SDM with the Laplace activation kernel of Oberauer's model space (Table 2): the same Gumbel noise and decision rule, with \(\kappa\) estimated freely. The density has a kink at \(\mu\), so estimating mu puts a kink at every response, which gradient-based sampling handles poorly; bmm() warns when the formula estimates mu.

Scaling of the activation

scaling decides how c translates into the activation of the target \(c^*\); the table in "What c means" gives the formulas. "density" divides c by the integral of \(s\) over the circle, so c weighs an activation of unit area. For the von Mises activation that integral is approximated by \(\sqrt{2\pi/\kappa}\), the form bmm has always used (the "sqrtexp" parametrization; c_sqrtexp2bessel() converts to Oberauer's exact Bessel form), and fits from before scaling existed are this cell. For the Laplace activation the integral is exact, \(2(1 - e^{-\kappa \pi}) / \kappa\); Oberauer (2023, eq. 2) multiplies by \(\kappa / 2\), which divides by the integral over the real line, \(2 / \kappa\). bmm keeps the exact integral over the circle, so its c is that of eq. 2 times \(1 - e^{-\kappa \pi}\) (0.998 at \(\kappa = 2\), 0.79 at \(\kappa = 0.5\)); c_laplace_circle2line() converts it to the c of eq. 2 and c_laplace_line2circle() back. "peak" takes c as the activation of the target, and "range" as the difference between the activation of the target and that of the location opposite it.

Default priors

kappa and c mean different things in each cell, so each cell has its own main priors (log scale; the effects and sd priors are the same everywhere). They were chosen in a prior predictive check so that the implied distributions of the circular SD of the response error are comparable across cells, not exactly matched. The last column is the share of prior predictive distributions with a circular SD below 0.05 radians; the Laplace cells still produce more of these spikes. The von Mises peak and range cells keep the priors of the default cell, which already give them comparable error distributions (Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance 0.06 to the default cell); the Laplace cells needed their own. Set your own priors where that matters.

activationscalingckappacircular SD < 0.05
"vonmises""density"student_t(5, 2, 0.75)student_t(5, 1.75, 0.75)0.07
"vonmises""peak"student_t(5, 2, 0.75)student_t(5, 1.75, 0.75)0.03
"vonmises""range"student_t(5, 2, 0.75)student_t(5, 1.75, 0.75)0.03
"laplace""density"student_t(5, 3.25, 0.75)student_t(5, -0.5, 0.75)0.16
"laplace""peak"student_t(5, 2.5, 0.75)student_t(5, -0.5, 0.75)0.11
"laplace""range"student_t(5, 2.25, 0.75)student_t(5, -0.5, 0.75)0.09

What c means

scaling\(c^*\), von Mises\(c^*\), Laplacec is
"density"\(c \sqrt{\kappa / 2\pi}\)\(c \kappa / (2 (1 - e^{-\kappa \pi}))\)the weight of an activation of unit area
"peak"\(c\)\(c\)the activation of the target
"range"\(c / (1 - e^{-2\kappa})\)\(c / (1 - e^{-\kappa \pi})\)the target-opposite contrast in activation

For a given data set the three scalings give the same likelihood at values of c related by these formulas; what differs is which quantity the regression formula for c and its prior act on.

Examples

if (FALSE) { # identical(Sys.getenv("BMM_EXAMPLES"), "true")
# simulate data from the model
dat <- data.frame(y = rsdm(n = 1000, c = 4, kappa = 3))

# specify formula
ff <- bmf(
  c ~ 1,
  kappa ~ 1
)

# specify the model
fit <- bmm(
  formula = ff,
  data = dat,
  model = sdm(resp_error = "y"),
  cores = 4,
  backend = "cmdstanr"
)
}
